title: Take One Tablet and Call Me in the Morning
bodyHtml:
Hittite is an extinct language that belongs to the Anatolian branch of the Indo-European language family. It was spoken in the ancient Hittite Empire in second millennium BCE. Hittite was written using a script, called cuneiform, composed of many wedge shapes; an example of cuneiform unrelated to this problem is below.

The excerpt below is a (simplified) phonetic rendering of a cuneiform passage found on a tablet. You do not need to know how the text is pronounced to solve this problem.

našta illuyankan
ḫattešnaz šarā kallišta
kāšawa ezenan iyami
nuwa adanna akuwanna eḫu

našta illuyankaš qadu dumumeššu
šarā úēr nuza eter ekuer
našta palḫan ḫūmandan ekuer
neza ninkēr

ne namma ḫattešnaš kattanta
nūmān pānzi ḫupašiyašša úit
nu illuyankan išḫimanta kalēliēt

imaš úit nukán illuyankan
kuenta dingirmešša kattišši ešer

Its translation into English:

And he called up the snake from the hole: “Behold the feast I’m making! Come to eat and to drink!” And the snake came up with his sons. And they ate and drank. And they drank all the kettles. And they could no longer go down into the hole again. And Hupasiyas came and tied the snake with a rope. The Stormgod came and killed the snake; and the gods were with him.”

F1

Match the following Hittite word forms with their English translations.

a. eter
b. ḫatteššar
c. úit
d. illuyankaš
e. našta
f. šarā
g. ekuer

(1) snake
(2) hole
(3) came
(4) and
(5) up
(6) drank
(7) ate

F2

Match the following suffixes with their grammatical roles.

a. –aš
b. –ša
c. –meš
d. –er/ēr
e. –an
f. –anna
g. –it

(1) marker of the infinitive (infinitives are verbs translated with to, such as “to sleep” or “to walk”)
(2) plural marker
(3) marker of 3rd person plural past tense verbs (these are past tense verbs with a subject of they or a plural noun, such as walked in “they walked” or drank in “the cats drank milk”)
(4) marker of the direct object (the direct object is the recipient of the action, such as him in “she hit him” or a pizza in “he made a pizza”)
(5) marker of the subject (the subject is the entity performing the action, such as the dog in “the dog chased the cat”)
(6) marker for 3rd person singular past tense verbs (these are past tense verbs with a subject of he, she, it, or a singular noun, such as walked in “he walked” or drank in “the cat drank milk”)
(7) marker denoting “and”

hints.text: The Hittite passage is laid out in four short stanzas, and the English translation follows the same order. Line the two up sentence by sentence before you try to identify single words: the first two Hittite lines correspond to “And he called up the snake from the hole”, and so on.

Look for the same root turning up with different endings. The root for “snake” appears three times, once as the one doing something and twice as the one being acted on. Similarly, the verb for “came” appears once with a single subject (Hupasiyas) and once with a plural subject (the snake with his sons). Comparing those pairs tells you what each ending does, and the differences also tell you which part of the word is the root.

Here is a worked step on a word that is not graded. The phrase ḫattešnaz šarā kallišta corresponds to “called up ... from the hole”. Since šarā is one word and kallišta is another, ḫattešnaz must carry both “hole” and “from” — that is, the ending –naz supplies the meaning “from”. Two useful lessons: Hittite packs grammatical relations into endings rather than separate little words, and the verb tends to come at the end of its clause.

explanationHtml:
Step 1: cut the text into sentences

The four Hittite stanzas run parallel to the English translation. Reading them side by side:

  • našta illuyankan ḫattešnaz šarā kallišta = “And he called up the snake from the hole”
  • kāšawa ezenan iyami = “Behold the feast I’m making!”
  • nuwa adanna akuwanna eḫu = “Come to eat and to drink!”
  • našta illuyankaš qadu dumumeššu šarā úēr = “And the snake came up with his sons”
  • nuza eter ekuer = “And they ate and drank”
  • našta palḫan ḫūmandan ekuer = “And they drank all the kettles”
  • ḫupašiyašša úit = “And Hupasiyas came”
  • nu illuyankan išḫimanta kalēliēt = “and tied the snake with a rope”
  • imaš úit nukán illuyankan kuenta = “The Stormgod came and killed the snake”
  • dingirmešša kattišši ešer = “and the gods were with him”

Step 2: the easy anchors

The word našta begins three lines, and each of those lines begins with “And” in English — so našta is a connector meaning “and”. šarā shows up in two lines, and both of those are the lines with “up” (“called up”, “came up”); everything else in those two lines is different, so šarā = “up”.

The root illuyanka- appears four times and “snake” appears four times in the translation, so that root means “snake”. That fixes illuyankaš as the “snake” form (F1.d).

Step 3: same root, different endings

Compare the two shapes of “snake”:

  • illuyankan in “he called up the snake” and “killed the snake” — here the snake is being acted upon, i.e. the direct object.
  • illuyankaš in “the snake came up” — here the snake is the one doing the action, i.e. the subject.

So –an marks the direct object (F2.e) and –aš marks the subject (F2.a). Notice that the word list in F1 gives ḫatteššar for “hole” — the plain, dictionary-like form, whereas in the text it appears as ḫattešnaz (“from the hole”) and ḫattešnaš. Because the root clearly means “hole”, F1.b is “hole”.

Step 4: singular versus plural verbs

Two forms of the verb “come” occur: úēr in “the snake came up with his sons” (two or more comers) and úit in “Hupasiyas came” and “The Stormgod came” (one comer). So úit is “came” with a singular subject (F1.c), and the difference between the two forms is the ending: –ēr/–er for “they did” (third person plural past) and –it for “he/she/it did” (third person singular past). That is F2.d and F2.g.

Now the line “And they ate and drank” contains exactly two verbs, eter and ekuer, both with the plural ending –er. Which is which? The next line, “And they drank all the kettles”, uses ekuer again — and its only verb is “drank”. So ekuer = “drank” (F1.g) and by elimination eter = “ate” (F1.a).

Step 5: the remaining suffixes

“Come to eat and to drink!” contains adanna akuwanna. Compare their roots with the past-tense verbs: ad- matches eter (“ate”) and akuw- matches ekuer (“drank”). What is left in each word is –anna, which therefore marks the infinitive, the “to eat / to drink” form (F2.f).

In “the snake came up with his sons” we find dumumeššu, and in “the gods were with him” we find dingirmešša. Both English phrases are plural (“sons”, “gods”) and both Hittite words contain –meš–, so –meš is the plural marker (F2.c).

Finally, two words end in –ša: ḫupašiyašša in “And Hupasiyas came” and dingirmešša in “and the gods were with him”. In both places the English has an extra “and” that no other Hittite word accounts for, so –ša is an attached “and” (F2.b). This kind of “and” that clings to the end of a word instead of standing alone is common in old Indo-European languages — Latin -que works the same way.

Answers

F1: a. (7) ate, b. (2) hole, c. (3) came, d. (1) snake, e. (4) and, f. (5) up, g. (6) drank.

F2: a. (5) subject, b. (7) “and”, c. (2) plural, d. (3) third person plural past, e. (4) direct object, f. (1) infinitive, g. (6) third person singular past.
